presentingComplaint: Subacute right-sided clumsiness, unsteadiness and double vision evolving over 4 days, on a background of hypertension — referred as a query posterior-circulation stroke.
history: Right-handed woman with a 6-year history of hypertension (on amlodipine) and dyslipidaemia, referred by A&E as a suspected brainstem stroke. Over 4 days she has developed progressively worsening horizontal diplopia, right-limb incoordination and gait unsteadiness — the deficit accrued gradually rather than at a single instant, and she was fully able to describe symptom onset while awake. On focused questioning she recalls a self-limiting episode of painful visual blurring in the left eye 9 years earlier (attributed to 'migraine' at the time) that recovered over 6 weeks, and a transient band of trunk numbness lasting 3 weeks two years ago that was never investigated. No headache, no thunderclap onset, no fever, no preceding infection, no seizures. Non-smoker. Her vascular risk factors and age initially anchored the team toward a vascular event, but the tempo, prior undiagnosed episodes and examination pattern do not fit a single vascular territory.
examination: Alert, orientated, no meningism. Cranial nerves: right internuclear ophthalmoplegia (impaired right eye adduction on left gaze with abducting nystagmus of the left eye) and mild left afferent pupillary defect with temporal disc pallor (old optic neuritis). Right dysmetria on finger-nose and heel-shin with an intention tremor; gait ataxic and wide-based, tandem impaired. Pyramidal pattern mild weakness right arm (MRC 4+/5), brisk reflexes globally, right extensor plantar. Reduced vibration to mid-shin bilaterally. Lhermitte phenomenon elicited on neck flexion. No aphasia, no cortical signs, no facial droop.
imaging: MRI brain with contrast: multiple T2/FLAIR hyperintense lesions, ovoid and periventricular with a perpendicular (Dawson-finger) orientation, plus juxtacortical and infratentorial (right middle cerebellar peduncle and dorsal pons) lesions. One periventricular and the pontine lesion show open-ring/incomplete-rim gadolinium enhancement (active), while others are non-enhancing — indicating lesions of differing ages. No vascular-territory infarct, no diffusion restriction on DWI, no mass effect. MRI cervical cord: short-segment (<2 vertebral bodies) dorsolateral demyelinating plaque at C4.
microbiology: Not applicable — no infective features; CSF bacterial culture and viral PCR panel negative.
differentialDiagnoses: Ischaemic stroke / posterior-circulation infarct (referral diagnosis; excluded by tempo, DWI-negative, multi-territory lesions of different ages)
Primary CNS vasculitis (excluded by normal inflammatory markers, negative ANCA/ANA, and lesion morphology)
Neoplasm / brainstem glioma (excluded by lack of mass effect and multifocal disseminated lesions)
finalDiagnosis: Multiple sclerosis, acute relapse (brainstem/cerebellar syndrome) — 2017 McDonald criteria met by dissemination in space and time with active and inactive lesions plus prior clinical episodes.
citations: International Panel / MAGNIMS — McDonald Diagnostic Criteria for Multiple Sclerosis — 2017
AAN — Disease-Modifying Therapies for Adults with Multiple Sclerosis — 2018
ECTRIMS/EAN — Pharmacological Treatment of Multiple Sclerosis — 2018
Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 22e — Multiple Sclerosis and Other Demyelinating Diseases
stewardship: Not applicable — non-infective demyelinating relapse. Acute relapse managed with high-dose corticosteroids (IV methylprednisolone 1 g/day for 3–5 days), not antibiotics.
contraindications: Exclude active infection before high-dose corticosteroids (steroid pseudorelapse/Uhthoff mimics)
Do not thrombolyse — this is not an acute ischaemic stroke despite the vascular risk profile and referral label
Screen for latent TB/hepatitis before initiating disease-modifying therapy
edgeCases: Late-onset MS (>50y) with vascular risk factors is readily mislabelled as small-vessel ischaemia; lesion morphology and DWI distinguish them
AQP4-IgG and MOG-IgG negativity helps exclude NMOSD/MOGAD (long-segment cord lesion would favour NMOSD)
A prior 'migrainous' visual episode was in fact unrecognised optic neuritis — supporting dissemination in time
expectedMaiK: Multifocal CNS demyelination disseminated in space and time on MRI (Dawson fingers, juxtacortical, infratentorial and cord lesions with both enhancing and non-enhancing plaques) in a DWI-negative, non-vascular pattern establishes MS relapse rather than stroke.
expectedNextQuestions: Any prior transient neurological episodes (visual loss, sensory bands, weakness) that recovered?
Does neck flexion trigger an electric-shock sensation down the spine (Lhermitte)?
Any heat-related transient worsening of symptoms (Uhthoff phenomenon)?
Was the onset instantaneous (stroke-like) or did it accrue over hours to days?
expectedInvestigations: MRI brain and whole spine with gadolinium (dissemination in space/time)
CSF analysis for oligoclonal bands and IgG index (unmatched to serum)
Serum AQP4-IgG and MOG-IgG to exclude NMOSD/MOGAD
Vasculitis/infective screen (ANA, ANCA, ESR/CRP, HIV, B12) to exclude mimics
